subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage: Sonali asked, “Sharmila, how did the science model go so wrong?” and Sharmila laughed. “Okay, listen. Our model volcano was due on Friday, and on Monday I sat and imagined it: paper mould one evening, paint the next, done by Wednesday. In my head nothing ever went wrong. So I started Tuesday night. The glue took a whole day to dry. The printer ran out of ink. The paint I wanted was finished at the shop, and I hadn't thought of any of that. Last year the same kind of project took me five days, not three, and I completely ignored that. I handed in a half-painted volcano on Friday and told myself it was a design choice.” 😅

qa.q: On which night did Sharmila start the model volcano?
qa.a: Sharmila started the volcano on Tuesday night.

qa.q: Why does Sharmila laugh while telling the story?
qa.a: Sharmila is laughing at the mistake and feeling a little embarrassed: the plan imagined everything going smoothly and ignored how last year's project had gone.

qa.q: What could Sharmila try next time before choosing a start date?
qa.a: Look at how long a similar project really took last year, and start earlier with time for glue drying and shop trips.

qa.q: What might Sonali be thinking as Sharmila tells this?
qa.a: Sonali is probably curious and amused, and perhaps recognising the same habit in Sonali's own projects.

grounding: A teenager estimates a project by imagining everything going smoothly and starts late as a result.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage: I'm Irfan, and I sit behind Pranav in history. When our teacher announced the essay on Thursday, Pranav told me, “Two evenings, easy. I know the topic.” I said nothing, because I remembered the map project in September, which he'd said would take one night and which took six days. On Sunday night Pranav was still gathering sources, and the second evening was gone before the introduction was done. I saw him on Monday morning, writing the conclusion on the school bus with his notebook on his knees. I don't know what he was thinking. He looked tired, but he also said, “It'll be fine.” The teacher gave it a mark he didn't seem to like.

qa.q: How many evenings did Pranav say the essay would take?
qa.a: Pranav said the essay would take two evenings.

qa.q: What might Pranav have been feeling on the school bus on Monday?
qa.a: Pranav seemed tired and perhaps worried, though “It'll be fine” suggests hopeful confidence; Irfan cannot be sure about Pranav's inner state.

qa.q: What could Pranav do before the next essay?
qa.a: Look back at how long the map project and this essay really took, and plan the start date from that instead of from the best-case picture.

qa.q: Why did Irfan say nothing about the map project?
qa.a: Irfan may have felt awkward correcting a classmate, and wanted to avoid sounding critical, so kept quiet.

grounding: A teenager estimates a project from the ideal story and starts late, seen by a classmate.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage: The school library was nearly empty at lunch. Aadhya had the geography project brief open: a model of a river basin, a report and a presentation, due in ten days. "It'll take a weekend," she told Ganga. "Saturday the model, Sunday the report." Ganga raised an eyebrow. "Remember the volcano model? The paint took three days to dry." Aadhya waved it off. "That was different. This time I'll be quick." She started the Saturday before the deadline. The clay cracked, the blue paint ran out, and the printer at the stationery shop was broken. On Monday she handed in the model with no report, her face hot.

qa.q: How many days did Aadhya have for the project?
qa.a: The project was due in ten days.

qa.q: Why did Aadhya wave off Ganga's reminder about the volcano model?
qa.a: She felt confident and hopeful, picturing everything going smoothly, so the earlier delay seemed like a one-off.

qa.q: What could Aadhya try next time she estimates a project?
qa.a: Aadhya could look at how long similar projects really took, like the volcano model, and start earlier to leave room for problems.

qa.q: How might Ganga feel watching Aadhya hand in the model without a report?
qa.a: Ganga might feel sorry for Aadhya and a little frustrated that the warning was ignored.

grounding: Shows a teenager estimating a project by imagining a smooth weekend and starting too late.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage:
Dear Saurabh bhaiya,

Remember you told me to start the science fair project early? I didn't. I thought, how hard can a solar oven be? Cardboard, foil, glass, done in one evening. So I started the night before.

The foil tore twice. The glue took forever to dry. Then I needed a thermometer to test it, and ours was broken. At midnight I had an oven that didn't cook anything. Ma had to write a note to the teacher.

Last year's kite project also took three evenings, not one. I just forgot that when I planned. Next time I'll start with that number.

Your brother,
Karthik

qa.q: What was Karthik's science fair project?
qa.a: It was a solar oven.

qa.q: How did Karthik feel planning the project, and how did that change?
qa.a: Karthik felt confident it would be done in one evening, and by midnight was frustrated and embarrassed, with an oven that didn't cook anything.

qa.q: What does Karthik plan to do differently?
qa.a: Karthik plans to use how long last year's kite project really took, three evenings, as the starting estimate.

qa.q: How might Saurabh bhaiya react to this letter?
qa.a: Saurabh bhaiya might feel sympathetic and a little amused, since the advice to start early is now proved right.

grounding: A teenager's letter shows planning from the ideal version of a project and ignoring how similar tasks went before.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage: Okay, so the podcast wants embarrassing school stories? I'm Jeevan, and here's mine. In Class Ten we had a history presentation, ten slides, due Friday. I thought, two hours on Thursday, easy. I imagined typing fast, finding perfect photos, nobody interrupting. My friend Damini had started on Monday. I laughed at her. On Thursday, the internet dropped, Amma needed help with the groceries, and I couldn't find a single photo of the right fort. By eleven I had four slides. I presented them with my voice shaking. Damini's were beautiful. That's when I figured out: the smooth version in my head never actually happens.

qa.q: How many slides was the presentation meant to have?
qa.a: It was meant to have ten slides.

qa.q: How did Jeevan feel presenting the four slides?
qa.a: Jeevan felt nervous and embarrassed, with a shaking voice, next to Damini's finished slides.

qa.q: What lesson could Jeevan use for the next project?
qa.a: Jeevan could plan for interruptions like the internet dropping and chores, and start early, as Damini did on Monday.

qa.q: How might Damini have seen Jeevan laughing at her early start?
qa.a: Damini may have felt a little teased but calm, trusting her own plan, and was proved right on Friday.

grounding: A teenager tells how imagining a smooth, interruption-free evening led to starting a project far too late.

subtopic: Estimating time and the planning fallacy
passage:
Monday. The inter-school short film contest wanted a three-minute film by Saturday. Rashmi pictured it all: film on Thursday after school, edit on Friday night, submit Saturday morning. "Two evenings, easy," she told her friend Bhupen. She didn't think of the last time, when a two-minute class video had taken a week.
Thursday. Rain. The park where she wanted to film was flooded. Bhupen had tuition till six. When they finally shot indoors at seven, the phone memory filled up after four scenes. They deleted old photos and shot again. The light was bad.
Saturday. Rashmi edited from midnight to 4 a.m. The music didn't match the scenes. The export failed twice. She submitted at 11:52, eight minutes before the deadline, with a jump in the sound she had no time to fix.
On the form, it asked, "How long did this take?" She laughed tiredly and wrote, "Longer than I imagined."

qa.q: By when did the contest want the film?
qa.a: By Saturday.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel as she typed on the form?
qa.a: Rashmi felt exhausted and a little rueful, laughing tiredly at how wrong the two-evening estimate had been.

qa.q: What could Rashmi have done when she first estimated the time?
qa.a: Rashmi could have remembered the class video that took a week and started filming earlier, with extra time for weather and technical problems.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have seen Rashmi's "Two evenings, easy"?
qa.a: Bhupen may have believed it at first, but by Thursday night Bhupen would have seen how much the plan ignored real problems.

grounding: Shows a teenager who estimates a film project from the smooth ideal story, starts late and ignores how similar tasks really went.
